title: The future of work
goals: Use the future perfect (simple and continuous) to talk about what will have happened, or what will have continued, up to a point in the future.
Use the future continuous for actions in progress in the future, and to ask politely about other people's plans.
Express what is imminent or scheduled with be about to, be due to, be on the verge of and be set to, without confusing them.
Grade the certainty of a prediction precisely (bound to, likely to, may well, unlikely to, there's every chance).
Talk about the working world with C1-level vocabulary: redundancy, freelance, burnout, upskill, gig economy.
Write predictions and proposals of 250 to 350 words about the future of work, in an analytical tone.

learn.title: Future perfect simple and continuous
learn.html:
This tense looks at the future “from ahead”: you place yourself at a point in the future and look back.

FormStructureExampleNuance
Future perfect simplewill have + past participleBy Friday I will have finished the report.An action finished before that point.
Future perfect continuouswill have been + -ingBy June I will have been working here for ten years.A duration that reaches up to that point; focus on the process.

Markers: by (+ time point), by the time (+ present clause), by then, in two years' time, before long. By means “no later than”; until means “up to” and describes a situation that continues: I'll wait until Friday versus I'll finish it by Friday.

The time-clause trap: after by the time, when, before, as soon as, once, will is NOT used: By the time I finish the degree, the market will have changed. In Spanish, the subjunctive (“cuando termine”, “when I finish”) causes the opposite mistake: when I will finish.

Other uses. The future perfect is also used to make a guess about the present or the very recent past, in a formal tone: You will have heard the news by now. Stative verbs do not usually take the continuous: will have known, not will have been knowing. In the negative there is a reading of “will not yet have…”: They won't have finished by then.

Simple or continuous: if you are interested in the result or the quantity, use the simple (will have written 300 pages); if the duration or the effort matters, use the continuous (will have been writing for two years).

watch.wrong: By the time I will finish, they will have left.
watch.right: By the time I finish, they will have left.
watch.why: After by the time, the present simple is used, not will.

watch.wrong: By next June I will work here for ten years.
watch.right: By next June I will have been working here for ten years.
watch.why: Duration up to a future point: future perfect (continuous).

watch.wrong: I will finish the report until Friday.
watch.right: I will finish the report by Friday.
watch.why: Until = up to (continuity); by = no later than.

watch.wrong: By 2030 she will have been knowing him for years.
watch.right: By 2030 she will have known him for years.
watch.why: Know is a stative verb: it does not take the continuous.

learn.title: Future continuous
learn.html:
Form: will be + verb-ing. Negative: won't be working. Question: Will you be working?

UseExampleNuance
Action in progress at a future momentThis time tomorrow I'll be flying to Lima.It paints a scene: “I will be flying”.
Action that will happen in the normal course of thingsThe CEO will be announcing the results on Monday.It sounds like something scheduled, not a spontaneous decision.
Polite question about someone else's plansWill you be using the projector this afternoon?Friendlier than Will you use…?, which can sound like a request or a decision.
Something that will still be true in the futureIn ten years many of us will still be working remotely.With still, it stresses continuity.

Will versus will be -ing. I'll call you is a decision taken now; I'll be calling you at six is a plan or routine already arranged. For a strong personal intention, I'm going to… is preferred.

Time clauses: just as with the future perfect, after when, while, as, before the present simple is used: When you arrive, I'll be waiting.

Stative verbs: stative verbs (know, understand, belong, own) do not take the continuous: I'll know the results by Friday.

watch.wrong: This time tomorrow I will fly to Madrid.
watch.right: This time tomorrow I will be flying to Madrid.
watch.why: An action in progress at a specific future moment: future continuous.

watch.wrong: When you will arrive, I will be waiting.
watch.right: When you arrive, I will be waiting.
watch.why: In a when clause, the present simple is used.

watch.wrong: I'll be knowing the results by Friday.
watch.right: I'll know the results by Friday.
watch.why: Know is a stative verb: it is not used in the continuous.

watch.wrong: Will you use the car tonight? (a polite question to a roommate)
watch.right: Will you be using the car tonight?
watch.why: “Will you use…?” sounds like a request or like demanding a plan; the continuous is neutral and polite.

learn.title: be about to, be due to, be on the verge of, be set to
learn.html:
Four ways to talk about what is about to happen, but each one says something different.

StructureNuanceExample
be about to + baseImminent, in the next few moments. It does not take a future time expression.Hurry up, the film is about to start.
be due to + baseScheduled or expected according to a timetable or plan.The new policy is due to come into effect in January.
be on the verge of + -ing / nounOn the brink of something important or dramatic (positive or negative).The firm is on the verge of bankruptcy. / She was on the verge of resigning.
be set to / be poised to + baseEverything is ready for it; journalistic and formal style.Unemployment is set to rise next year.

Watch the preposition. Be due to + base (“is scheduled to”) is not the same as the preposition due to + noun (“because of”): The delay was due to a strike. And on the verge of takes -ing or a noun, never an infinitive.

About to and past tenses. I was about to call you when… (“I was on the point of calling you when…”) is used for interrupted or avoided actions. English has no single general expression for this, so it requires a choice: about to (seconds), on the verge of (critical moment), due to (timetable).

watch.wrong: The plane is about to land in ten minutes.
watch.right: The plane is due to land in ten minutes.
watch.why: About to does not take a future time frame; for something scheduled, use due to.

watch.wrong: He's on the verge to resign.
watch.right: He's on the verge of resigning.
watch.why: On the verge of + -ing, not an infinitive.

watch.wrong: The law is due to being passed next year.
watch.right: The law is due to be passed next year.
watch.why: Be due to + infinitive (here in the passive: to be passed).

learn.title: Degrees of certainty in predictions
learn.html:
Predicting well in English is not just a matter of using will. There is a scale of certainty, and each point has its own structures.

DegreeStructuresExample
Almost certainwill definitely / is bound to / is sure (certain) to / there is no doubt thatAutomation is bound to change logistics.
Probablewill probably / is likely to / in all likelihood / is set toMany offices are likely to adopt hybrid schedules.
Possiblemay / might / could (well) / there's a chance thatThe company may well relocate.
Unlikelyis unlikely to / is hardly likely to / I doubt whether / there's little chance thatThe four-day week is unlikely to reach every sector.

Nuances. May well and might well raise the probability compared with may and might. Likely is used with be likely to + base or it is likely that…; there is no *be probable to*: one says it is probable that… (formal) or will probably. Bound to expresses an almost logical consequence (She's bound to get the job).

Adverb position. With will, the adverb goes before the main verb: will probably / definitely go; in the negative it goes before the auxiliary: probably won't. Perhaps and maybe go at the beginning.

Caution. In academic and journalistic texts, is expected to, is projected to, is forecast to and phrases such as there is every chance that are preferred. Note: after doubt in an affirmative sentence we use whether/that: I doubt that many will return. Avoid adding a negative after doubt, as happens in literal translations: I doubt that many won't return is misleading.

watch.wrong: AI is bound replace many routine jobs.
watch.right: AI is bound to replace many routine jobs.

watch.wrong: Robots are probable to take over routine tasks.
watch.right: Robots are likely to take over routine tasks.
watch.why: Be probable to does not exist: use be likely to or will probably.

watch.wrong: She may well to change her mind.
watch.right: She may well change her mind.

watch.wrong: He will for sure to get the contract.
watch.right: He will definitely get the contract.
watch.why: Certainty adverbs go before the verb; no to after will.

learn.title: Functions: predicting and grading certainty
learn.html:
• Almost certain: There's no doubt that… / It's bound to… / I'm convinced that… will…
  • Probable: It's highly likely that… / In all likelihood… / I'd expect… to…
  • Possible: It could well… / There's a fair chance that… / It's entirely possible that…
  • Unlikely: It's unlikely that… / I doubt whether… / There's little prospect of…
  • Timeframes and projections: By 2040, … will have… / Within a decade, … / In the long run, … / Sooner or later…
  • Introducing caution: It remains to be seen whether… / Only time will tell. / That said, … / Having said that, …
  • Talking about what is imminent: The firm is on the verge of… / The deal is due to be signed… / We're about to…

write.prompt: Write an essay of 250-350 words predicting how your profession (or one you know well) will look in 2040. Use different degrees of certainty, mention at least one factor like automation, remote work or reskilling, and refer to what will have changed by then and what will still be happening. Organise your ideas into 3-4 paragraphs with a clear opening and conclusion.
checklist: 250-350 words in 3-4 paragraphs, with an introduction and a conclusion
At least one future perfect (simple or continuous) with by 2040 or by then
At least one future continuous (will still be -ing)
Three different degrees of certainty (bound to, likely to, may well, unlikely to)
Five work-related vocabulary items (redundancy, upskill, workforce, labour market...)
Present simple after by the time / when / before
Hedging connectors (That said, It remains to be seen...)
write.model:
By 2040, the teaching profession will look very different from the one I joined fifteen years ago. Few people doubt that technology will reshape the classroom, but the real question is how far it will change what teachers actually do.

Automation is bound to take over much of the routine work. By the time today's primary pupils leave school, adaptive software will have taken over most marking and basic exercises, which will free teachers to concentrate on discussion, mentoring and creativity. Remote work is likely to become standard for certain tasks too: lesson planning and parent meetings will probably be held online, and some specialist subjects may well be taught by experts connecting from the other side of the world. That said, it is unlikely that machines will replace the human relationship at the heart of learning.

The labour market will also demand constant reskilling. By 2040 the average teacher will have retrained at least twice, and many will be upskilling every summer in data analysis and digital pedagogy. Schools that fail to invest in their workforce may face redundancies, while those that adapt will attract the best graduates. It remains to be seen whether governments will fund this transition fairly.

Even so, some things will not have changed. Teachers will still be managing restless teenagers, and they will still be answering questions that no algorithm anticipated. When the next generation of pupils arrives, they will be looking for someone who notices when they are struggling. In short, technology will transform the tools of the profession, but the heart of it will remain stubbornly human.

write.prompt: Write a formal email of 250-350 words to the Human Resources director of a company proposing a reskilling programme for employees whose tasks are likely to be automated. Explain the situation, make predictions with appropriate caution, say what the company is about to do or is due to do, and propose three concrete steps.
targets: be about to / be due to / be on the verge of
checklist: 250-350 words with a formal greeting, body and sign-off
A structure for an imminent or scheduled future (be due to, be set to, be on the verge of)
Two predictions with different degrees of certainty
A well-formed future perfect or future continuous
Vocabulary: upskill, redundancy, workforce, skill set, transferable skills
Three concrete proposals, clearly numbered or linked
Formal tone, without excessive contractions and without by/until errors
write.model:
Dear Ms Alvarez,

I am writing to propose a reskilling programme for employees whose roles are likely to be automated over the coming years.

As you are aware, our company is due to introduce automated invoicing and customer-service tools in the third quarter, and the finance department is on the verge of a significant restructuring. Our competitors have already moved in this direction. It is almost certain that routine data entry will have disappeared from most departments by the end of 2027, and it is quite possible that further tasks will follow. We should therefore not wait until redundancies become unavoidable.

I would like to suggest three concrete steps. First, we could carry out a skills audit across the workforce to identify which tasks are most exposed and which transferable skills each employee already possesses, so that every skill set can be matched against future needs. Second, we might establish a six-month upskilling programme, delivered partly online and partly during working hours, in areas such as data analysis, project coordination and client relations. Third, we should create an internal mobility scheme, so that those who complete the programme are given priority when new positions open.

I appreciate that such an initiative requires investment. Nevertheless, retraining existing staff is likely to prove considerably cheaper than recruiting and training replacements, and it would help us retain valuable knowledge. By this time next year, we could be running the first cohort, and the company will have demonstrated its commitment to its people.

I would welcome the opportunity to discuss these proposals in more detail at your convenience, and I can prepare a costed outline if that would be helpful.

Yours sincerely,

Daniel Reyes
Operations Analyst

reading.title: The Quiet Revolution at Halden & Moss
reading.intro: Read the feature article and answer the questions.
paragraphs: When the logistics firm Halden & Moss announced, last spring, that it was on the verge of scrapping the five-day week, most of its competitors assumed it was a publicity stunt. Six months on, nobody is laughing. The trial, which was due to end in September, has been extended until the end of the year, and the managers who were the most sceptical are now among its strongest defenders.

The arrangement is simple. Staff work four days, keep their full salary and are expected to deliver the same results. There is, inevitably, a catch: meetings have been slashed, email is discouraged after five and employees are asked to map out their week in advance. Priya Nair, who heads the operations team, admits she was about to hand in her notice when the scheme was introduced. 'I had been working sixty-hour weeks for three years,' she says. 'I was on autopilot. By the time the trial started, I'd more or less forgotten what a free Friday felt like.'

The early figures are encouraging. Sick leave has fallen by nearly a third, and the number of resignations is down. Productivity, the metric that sceptics were most keen to cite, has barely moved, which, the company argues, is precisely the point. Yet researchers who study working patterns urge caution. A trial run by a motivated firm, they point out, is bound to produce rosier results than a nationwide rollout, because the staff know they are being watched and are therefore inclined to behave well. 'It may well work for knowledge-based roles,' says labour economist Dr Tomás Ibarra. 'Whether it will work for a hospital ward or a factory floor is a different question.'

Automation complicates the picture further. Halden & Moss has quietly introduced software that handles invoicing and scheduling, tasks that used to occupy a team of six. Rather than laying those employees off, the firm has offered them retraining, and most have accepted. 'Nobody will have the same job in ten years' time,' admits the chief executive, Marguerite Holt. 'The question is whether we'll still be employing the same people, and I'd like to think we will. The alternative is a workforce that wakes up one morning to find its skills obsolete.'

Critics remain unconvinced that such generosity can last. If a downturn arrives, they argue, even the most progressive employers will be tempted to cut costs by cutting staff. Others fear a two-tier labour market in which well-paid professionals enjoy shorter weeks while gig workers, with no safety net, work longer for less. Both concerns are legitimate, and neither has been answered. Still, as the trial approaches its final month, one thing seems clear: the assumption that more hours automatically mean more output has been shaken. By this time next year, if the early results hold, a good many of Halden & Moss's rivals will have been forced to follow suit, or to explain why they have not. For workers, the significance may be larger still. If a four-day week proves workable in logistics, a notoriously demanding industry, it becomes much harder for other employers to argue that it is simply impossible. Whether that argument will be won on evidence, or merely on fashion, is a question that employees, managers and economists will all be watching closely in the months ahead.

listening.title: The Career Clinic
listening.intro: Listen to the radio programme. You can repeat it.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Career Clinic. With me today are Nadia Okafor, a career coach, and Ben Cole, who left a stable corporate job to go freelance. Ben, by this time next year you'll have been working for yourself for two years. Any regrets?
Honestly, none so far, though I'd be lying if I said it was a smooth ride. In the first six months I was on the verge of going back more than once.
That's incredibly common. People underestimate how long it takes for freelance income to stabilise. Most advice says to have at least six months' salary saved before you jump.
Nadia, you work with a lot of people in mid-career. What are you hearing from them at the moment?

Anxiety about automation, mostly. A lot of my clients are convinced their jobs will have vanished within ten years. I tell them that's unlikely for most roles, but it's almost certain that the tasks within those roles will change.
That's what I found. I used to spend half my week on admin. Now software does it in minutes, and I'm free to concentrate on the creative side, which is what clients actually pay for.
Enormously. Not necessarily a whole new degree, mind you. Even a short course can make you stand out. I always say: don't wait until you're made redundant to start learning.
Hear, hear. I'm doing a data analysis course at the moment. This time next month, I'll be sitting my first exam, and I'm absolutely dreading it.
Is there a downside to all this flexibility? I'm thinking of burnout.
Absolutely. When your office is your kitchen table, work tends to seep into every corner of your life. Setting boundaries isn't optional; it's survival.
I'm still working on that. My partner says I'm bound to burn out if I keep answering emails at midnight, and she's probably right.
On that sobering note, a short break, and then we'll take your calls.

tasks.prompt: Predict how your profession (or one you know well) will change over the next fifteen years.
questions: What do you do, or what would you like to do?
How is your field likely to change by 2040?
Which of your current tasks might be automated?
What skills will people in your field need to learn?
tasks.model: I work in finance, and I'm convinced the sector is bound to change dramatically. By 2040, routine tasks like reconciliations will almost certainly have been automated, and analysts will be spending far more time interpreting data. Many roles may well disappear, but I suspect new ones will emerge. People who don't upskill are unlikely to keep pace.
checklist: Use a future perfect (will have been automated)
Use a future continuous (will be spending)
Two different degrees of certainty (bound to, may well, unlikely to)
Work vocabulary (upskill, sector, roles)

tasks.prompt: Talk about where you plan to be in five years and what you will have achieved.
questions: Where do you expect to be working in five years?
What will you have achieved by then?
What will you be doing on a typical day?
What might get in the way?
tasks.model: In five years' time I hope to be leading a small team. By then I'll have completed a master's degree and I'll have been working for the same company for almost eight years. On a typical day, I'll probably be managing projects rather than doing the technical work myself. The main obstacle is that the firm may well restructure, but I'm optimistic.
checklist: Future perfect and future perfect continuous
Future continuous for a typical day
A certainty structure (will probably, may well)
Connectors and a natural closing

tasks.prompt: Debate: should every company adopt a four-day working week?
questions: Do you think a four-day week is realistic for most companies?
Would you personally prefer it, and why?
tasks.model: I think it's likely to work well for office-based roles, but I doubt whether it will suit sectors like healthcare, where shifts are essential. That said, there's every chance that productivity will hold steady, because people tend to focus better when they're rested. Personally, I'd welcome it, though it remains to be seen whether employers will be willing to go along.
checklist: Degrees of certainty (likely to, I doubt whether, there's every chance)
A contrast connector (That said, However)
A hedging formula (it remains to be seen)
A justified personal opinion
